idea: Four words stacked in descending weight, wispy to heavy: 'cirrus' (curl of hair), 'cumulus' (heap), 'stratus' (layer), 'nimbus' (rain), each with its Latin meaning in tiny caps, signed 'Luke Howard, pharmacist, 1802'. A pharmacist gave the sky its vocabulary, and anyone who looks up wants to own that.

Lewis Fry Richardson's 1922 verse, set as a spiral that shrinks to a point: 'Big whorls have little whorls, which feed on their velocity, and little whorls have lesser whorls, and so on to viscosity.' It is a real turbulence line, a parody of Swift's fleas, and it suits anyone who likes science with wit.

Plain stacked lettering: 'Richardson, 1922. Six hours of weather. Six weeks of arithmetic. Wrong by 145 hectopascals. He then imagined 64,000 people in a hall doing it faster.' A true, funny origin story of numerical forecasting, on a shirt for the forecast-sceptic and the forecast-lover.

A column of Beaufort numbers 0 to 12 in growing, increasingly battered type, using the sailor's original sail wording: '1 Just sufficient to give steerage' down to '12 That which no canvas could withstand'. Letterforms get more ragged with each force.

The shipping-forecast sea areas as a dense typographic chart: Dogger, Fisher, German Bight, Viking, Forties, Cromarty, Forth, Tyne, Humber, Thames, Dover, Wight, Portland, Plymouth, Biscay, FitzRoy, Sole, Lundy, Fastnet, Rockall, Malin, Hebrides, Bailey, Fair Isle. A litany for people who find the broadcast a kind of poetry; FitzRoy, who coined the word 'forecast', is on the list.

One big word, 'PETRICHOR', letters beaded with drops, with small print: 'The smell of rain on dry ground. Named in 1964 by two Australian chemists, from the Greek for stone and the blood of the gods.' A true, lovely word with a story.

A weather-app icon turned into an equation: '30% chance of rain = PoP = C x A', with the footnote 'confidence that it will rain somewhere in the forecast area, times the fraction of the area that gets wet.' Almost everyone misreads it, and the shirt corrects them in a nerdy way.

Huge numerals '100-YEAR FLOOD' with the line below: '1% chance. Every single year. Not once a century.' A hard-edged correction of a common misunderstanding, for people who like being right about risk.

A giant Greek capital Delta with a tiny caption: 'Herodotus named it for the fourth letter of the alphabet, because the mouth of the Nile looked like one.' The first geographic term taken from a letter; the triangle is the whole design.

The word 'meander' set along a looping river line that pinches into an oxbow, with the caption 'From the Maeander, a winding river in Turkey.' Typography that behaves like its subject, with a true etymology.

Small centered lettering: 'Einstein, 1926: why rivers meander. The answer is in your teacup.' (Tea leaves gather in the middle of a stirred cup for the same reason a river bends: the secondary flow on the bed.) A quiet, true, little-known paper to wear.

Mark Twain's arithmetic as a column of figures: 'Cairo to New Orleans: 1,215 miles. After the cutoffs: 973. Shortened 242 miles in 176 years.' Twain extrapolated it into a joke about the future (Life on the Mississippi, 1883); the shirt gives the river's side of the story.

Two words in opposed weights running side by side without touching: 'RIO NEGRO' in black and 'SOLIMOES' in white, captioned 'Meeting of the Waters. Six kilometres side by side before they agree.' The two Amazon tributaries really do flow unmixed for miles because of differences in temperature, speed and density.

Lightning drawn only in type: the numbers '30,000 K' in a jagged zigzag, the small line 'The sun's surface: 5,800.' Lightning really is several times hotter than the sun's surface; a shirt that makes the comparison in few words.
A grid of round drops, with one correction in bold: 'Raindrops are not tear-shaped.' Smaller ones are spheres, larger ones flatten like hamburger buns. Everyone has drawn them wrong since childhood.

A proverb in two tones: 'Red sky at night, sailors' delight.' underneath, small: 'It works because weather in mid-latitudes moves west to east, and the setting sun lights the clear air behind it.' A folk saying with a real mechanism behind it.

Admiral FitzRoy's storm barometer lines in engraved capitals: 'LONG FORETOLD, LONG LAST; SHORT NOTICE, SOON PAST.' Real text from his barometers; a weather proverb with a Victorian instrument-maker's voice.
A fluffy-lettered word 'CUMULUS' with the line 'About 500 tonnes of water. Floating.' A fair-weather cumulus is estimated at roughly that much; the shirt is a small shock for anyone looking up.

'BLOW, WINDS, AND CRACK YOUR CHEEKS! RAGE! BLOW!' (King Lear, III.ii) set in giant letters that lean left, with the first word stretched by the gale. Shakespeare's storm needs no joke, only typography with weather in it.

Christina Rossetti's 1872 lines set as a column that sways: 'Who has seen the wind? Neither I nor you: But when the leaves hang trembling, The wind is passing through.' The wind drawn as a letter-by-letter lean in the words themselves; one of the best short poems on weather.
